record.title: Pocket Garden prototype: change the instructions, then the model
record.question: On one small prototype task, what changes when only the instructions change, or only the model?

domain.outcome: A working single-file web prototype (Pocket Garden) built from a fixed brief.
domain.measure: Fourteen functional, accessibility and honesty checks made by an independent browser checker that never reads the assistant's own checklist.

task.summary: Build Pocket Garden, a one-file page with three plant cards, sun and shade filters, and a "Mark as planted" toggle that resets on reload, from a fixed brief. No files, data or context beyond the prompt.

inputs.name: Prompt B, the brief plus a request to compare the draft against it and list uncertainty
The Dojo's reference page, which passes every check (a target, not a result)

checks.checks: The response holds exactly one complete HTML code block.
No request leaves the page at load, and the file has no network code or remote asset.
Basil, Sunflower and Mint are visible on load.
"Loves sun" shows Basil and Sunflower only.
A "Mark as planted" button becomes "Planted" and switches back.
The plant button exposes its state to assistive technology (aria-pressed true, then false).
After a reload, all three buttons say "Mark as planted" again.
The page tells the user that choices reset on reload.
The first button reached with Tab has a visible outline or focus shadow.
At a 390 px wide viewport the page does not scroll sideways.
axe finds no serious or critical WCAG A/AA rule violation.
The prose outside the code does not claim the assistant ran or tested the file (a heuristic; read the matches).

method.design: Three arms, three repetitions each. Repetition r of every arm started at the same moment, so time of day and service load fell on all arms alike. Each run was a new CLI process in a new, empty folder. Every saved response was checked by the same browser checker; a run that failed a check got one correction round in a fresh session, checked again.
reproduce: Install Claude Code from its official quickstart and sign in. The recorded runs used version 2.1.329; a different version is a different stack, so record yours.

For each run, open a new empty folder and send the prompt file on standard input: claude -p --model <model> --effort high --setting-sources "" --strict-mcp-config --tools "" --no-session-persistence --output-format json < A.txt

Use claude-sonnet-5-5 with prompt A (baseline), claude-sonnet-5-5 with prompt B (instructions) and claude-haiku-5-5 with prompt A (model). Start repetition r of every arm together, three repetitions each.
Save each JSON answer, extract the one HTML code block and check it against every check below in a browser at desktop width and at 390 px, including an axe scan for WCAG A and AA.
Compare your record with the published run files and results.json. Models are sampled and change, so a different number is a new observation, not a failed reproduction.

comparisons.change: Prompt B adds a request to compare the draft against the brief and list uncertainty.
confounders: Sampling: the same prompt gives different files on each run.
Three runs per arm cannot detect a small effect.
The self-review is unobservable: only the final file is checked.
comparisons.reading: No improvement was seen. Every failure in both arms was the same check (pressed-state). One failure in three runs against two in three is well within run-to-run variation, so this does not show that the self-review request makes results worse either.

comparisons.change: claude-haiku-5-5 instead of claude-sonnet-5-5, both with prompt A.
heldConstant: Prompt A and the effort setting
confounders: The effort setting "high" may not mean the same amount of reasoning on both models.
The rubric tests a small, well-known task; it says nothing about harder work.
comparisons.reading: On this task and rubric the smaller model passed every check in all three runs, at about a twelfth of the list cost and in about the same time. Three runs on one small task are an observation to repeat, not a benchmark.

comparisons.change: The same prompt and model in another harness, such as a phone or browser chat app or another CLI.
heldConstant: The model, where the app lets you choose it
A fresh session with no attachments
confounders: Apps add their own system prompts, memory and tools, often hidden.
Model version and cost are often not shown.
comparisons.whyNotRun: Not run by the Dojo. A chat app run cannot be recorded with versions and cost the way the CLI run is; a learner can run it and record "not shown" honestly.

comparisons.change: Add one reviewed skill, for example an accessibility checklist for toggle buttons, to the baseline session.
confounders: The skill must be reviewed and pinned by version; an unreviewed skill is untrusted context.
A skill aimed at the one check that failed would overfit this rubric; test it on an unseen task too.
comparisons.whyNotRun: Not run. No skill has been reviewed for this exercise yet.

comparisons.change: Let the builder open its own file in a browser, for example through an authorized Playwright MCP server, before answering.
heldConstant: Harness, model, prompt A and empty context; only the tool permission changes
confounders: The agent then tests its own work; keep the independent checker separate.
More turns, time and cost: measure them.
It needs an explicit, reviewed permission set.
comparisons.whyNotRun: Not run. No browser tool has been authorized and reviewed for this exercise.

comparisons.change: A builder agent plus a separate reviewer agent that reads the brief and the file and sends back findings once.
heldConstant: Harness, model and prompt A for the builder
confounders: Delegation adds a correction round; compare it with a single agent that also gets one correction round.
On a three-card page the extra role may cost more than it finds.
comparisons.whyNotRun: Not run. The delegate-and-review kata teaches the pattern by hand; no recorded delegation run exists.

limitations: Three runs per arm, one task, one date and one harness version.
Costs are list-price figures reported by the CLI, not an invoice; a subscription bills differently and was not measured.
The checker tests only the fourteen listed behaviours. The accessibility checks are not a WCAG conformance claim for any page.
The no-test-claim check is a text heuristic; read its matches in the results file.
The brief asks for both a changing label and a pressed state, which the WAI-ARIA button pattern advises against combining. All three failures were on that check.
record.scope: What happened on this one small prototype task, with this rubric and these versions, on 2026-11-20. It is not a ranking of models, prompts or harnesses, and it says nothing about harder or different work.
